curatorBrief.title: Welcome to Pattern Power!
curatorBrief.intent: Introduce Grade 1 students to repeating and growing patterns using colorful shapes, counting blocks, and relatable sequences. Outline our three missions: copying repeating patterns, identifying what comes next by finding the core rule, and building our own growing patterns.

objectives.objectiveText: Copy and continue repeating patterns using real objects like colored blocks or shapes

componentConfigs.title: What Makes a Pattern?
componentConfigs.intent: Introduce key terms with bright visuals: 'Repeating Pattern' (something that repeats over and over), 'Unit / Core' (the part that repeats), and 'Continue' (adding what comes next).
componentConfigs.description: A set of 3-4 distinct key terms or concepts defined with visuals. Use for vocabulary or core principles.

componentConfigs.title: Copy and Continue Patterns
componentConfigs.intent: Engage students in copying and extending repeating patterns using colored blocks and geometric shapes (AB, AAB, ABB, and ABC patterns) to build tactile and visual continuity.
componentConfigs.description: Interactive pattern recognition, extension, and creation for K-3 algebraic thinking. Students build, extend, identify cores, translate, and create repeating patterns (AB, AAB, ABC), growing patterns (1,3,5,7), and number patterns. Supports color tokens, shape tokens, and numbers. Progressive phases: Copy → Identify → Create → Translate. Connects pattern skills to skip counting, multiplication foundations, and early algebra. ESSENTIAL for grades K-3 algebraic thinking, pattern recognition, and early algebra foundations.

componentConfigs.title: Say the Pattern Rule
componentConfigs.intent: The live tutor shows a visual pattern (e.g., star, circle, star, circle) and prompts the student to say out loud which shape comes next and name the repeating rule.
componentConfigs.description: Live-judged Direct Instruction practice for ANY skill whose answer is one short SPOKEN word or phrase: the tutor asks a scripted question out loud, the child ANSWERS ALOUD (voice/microphone), and the tutor judges the audio in-band. The stimulus is generated per objective — printed text, a picture, a group of pictures to count, or nothing at all (the tutor says it). Use this when the skill is genuinely verbal and there is NO manipulative the child needs to touch: recall answers, reading a short printed item aloud, counting a group and saying how many, saying which word from a set the objective NAMES (longer/shorter, heavier/lighter) describes two things shown side by side, and — for explain / describe / tell-why objectives — saying IN THEIR OWN WORDS what a shown instance means or what rule it follows (what the equal sign means, the rule of a pattern), judged on meaning rather than wording. ESSENTIAL where a tutor-driven spoken loop is the right modality but no bespoke primitive exists.
evalModeSkills: explain_concept: The child sees one instance (an equation on a balance, a pattern, a ten rod) and says in their own words what it means or what rule it follows. Use for explain / describe / tell-why objectives whose answer is a short idea with many correct wordings. Judged on meaning; the ask never states the concept.

cards.title: Repeating Pattern
cards.subheading: A line of shapes or colors that repeats again and again!
cards.definition: A repeating pattern is an orderly line of items, like colored blocks or shapes, arranged so that the exact same sequence happens over and over without changing.

conceptElements.detail: Red, Blue, Red, Blue shows a 2-part repeating sequence.
conceptElements.label: Simple Example

conceptElements.detail: Because it repeats, you can always guess what block belongs where!
conceptElements.label: Predictable Order

cards.timelineContext: Step 1 in Pattern Power: Spotting when a row of blocks follows a repeating rule rather than random mixing.
cards.originStory: Ancient basket weavers discovered that alternating light reeds and dark reeds in the same order made their woven baskets strong, durable, and eye-catching.
cards.curiosityNote: You can make a repeating pattern with sounds! Try clapping and tapping your knees: Clap, Tap, Clap, Tap!
cards.visualPrompt: A straight row of bright wooden blocks on a clean desk: Red cube, Blue sphere, Red cube, Blue sphere, Red cube, Blue sphere lined up evenly.

cards.title: Pattern Core (The Unit)
cards.subheading: The special chunk that repeats to build the whole pattern!
cards.definition: The core is the shortest group of blocks or shapes that repeats. Once you find the core, you have found the secret recipe of the pattern.

conceptElements.detail: The core is the smallest chunk that repeats from start to finish.
conceptElements.label: The Building Block

conceptElements.detail: In Yellow-Green-Green, Yellow-Green-Green, the core is Yellow-Green-Green.
conceptElements.label: Core Example

conceptElements.detail: Put your fingers around the first full repeat to isolate the core.
conceptElements.label: Find the Unit

cards.timelineContext: Step 2 in Pattern Power: Finding the repeating core so you know the exact rule of the pattern.
cards.originStory: Printmakers carve one single stamp design and press it repeatedly across fabric to make wallpaper and clothing prints.
cards.curiosityNote: A core can be 2 blocks long (AB), 3 blocks long (ABC or AAB), or even longer!
cards.visualPrompt: Snap cubes connected in a row: Yellow, Green, Green, Yellow, Green, Green. A bright glowing dotted rectangle frames the first Yellow, Green, Green set to show it as the core.

cards.title: Continue the Pattern
cards.subheading: Add the correct next blocks to keep the line going!
cards.definition: To continue a pattern means to look back at the repeating core and add the correct block or shape that comes next in the sequence.

conceptElements.detail: Say the pattern out loud to hear what block should land in the blank spot.
conceptElements.label: Ask What Comes Next

conceptElements.detail: Check if your new piece matches the start of the core.
conceptElements.label: Match the Core

conceptElements.detail: Place your block down and read the whole row again to make sure it sounds right.
conceptElements.label: Check Your Work

cards.timelineContext: Step 3 in Pattern Power: Using the core to extend, copy, and complete the row with your hands.
cards.originStory: Masons building brick walls learned that following the pattern layer by layer ensured the wall never tipped over.
cards.curiosityNote: As long as you have enough colored blocks, you can continue a repeating pattern all the way across your classroom floor!
cards.visualPrompt: A child's hand placing an orange plastic triangle into an empty spot at the end of a colorful shape line: Orange Triangle, Blue Hexagon, Orange Triangle, Blue Hexagon, with a glowing empty outline waiting for the next piece.

data.title: Kitchen Counter Pattern Lab: Repeating and Growing Patterns
data.subject: Math
data.overview: Become a pattern detective right in your own kitchen! By sorting and arranging everyday treasures like dried pasta, buttons, or coins, you will discover the secrets of repeating sequences and growing mathematical towers.
learningObjectives: Identify, describe, and extend simple repeating patterns (such as AB, ABB, and ABC) using physical objects and rhythmic speech.
Distinguish between repeating patterns and growing patterns by observing changes in quantity.
Create and predict the next term in a growing pattern using counting and visual models.

substitutes: a straight edge of a kitchen table

steps.title: Sort Your Treasure Collection
steps.instruction: Place your different counters into separate small bowls so each kind of object has its own home.
steps.tip: Keep each group separated clearly so you can grab items quickly when building your sequence.

steps.title: Build an AB Repeating Train
steps.instruction: Line up your objects in an AB pattern along your paper strip by alternating one of Type A, then one of Type B, and repeat: A, B, A, B, A, B.

checkpoint.question: Touch each item and read it aloud with a rhythm: 'Bow-tie, Macaroni, Bow-tie, Macaroni!' Does your rhythm stay the same?

steps.scienceNote: The 'core unit' is the shortest chunk that repeats. Here, the unit is just two items: [A, B].

steps.title: Level Up to an ABB Pattern
steps.instruction: Clear your line. Now build a new sequence using one Type A object followed by two Type B objects: A, B, B, A, B, B, A, B, B.

checkpoint.question: How many items are in one complete core unit of an ABB pattern?

steps.tip: Try whispering the single item and clapping twice for the double item to feel the rhythm.

steps.title: The Disappearing Piece Mystery
steps.instruction: Close your eyes while your helper removes one object from your pattern. Open your eyes, chant the pattern out loud, and guess the missing piece.

checkpoint.question: What clues did the neighboring pieces give you to help identify the missing object?

steps.title: Switch to a Growing Pattern
steps.instruction: Clear your line to start something new! Place 1 penny in the first row. Directly underneath, make a second row with 2 pennies. Make a third row with 3 pennies.
steps.scienceNote: Repeating patterns repeat the same cycle again and again, but growing patterns change by a regular mathematical rule each step.

steps.title: Predict and Extend the Growth
steps.instruction: Look closely at your penny staircase. Use your counters to build the 4th row and the 5th row following the same growth rule.

checkpoint.question: How many counters did you need to make the 5th row?

steps.tip: Notice how each step adds exactly one more counter than the step before it.

reflectionPrompts.question: What is the difference between how your pasta train looked in Step 2 compared to how your penny staircase looked in Step 5?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Distinguish between repeating patterns and growing patterns by observing changes in quantity.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether the sizes stay the same or get bigger and bigger as you move forward.

reflectionPrompts.question: If you wanted to build the 10th row of your growing staircase, how could you figure out how many counters you need without building all the rows first?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Create and predict the next term in a growing pattern using counting and visual models.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look at the row number and compare it to the number of counters in that row.

reflectionPrompts.question: Where can you spot repeating patterns or growing patterns in your daily life or nature?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Identify, describe, and extend simple repeating patterns using physical objects.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look at bathroom tiles, clothing stripes, tree branches, or musical beats.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Take a photo looking down at your finished growing staircase alongside your favorite repeating pattern chain.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: My pattern lab results! My repeating pattern rule was ______ and row 5 of my growing pattern had ______ pieces!

extensions.title: The Double-Growth Tower
extensions.description: Create a growing pattern that adds 2 items each time instead of 1 (Row 1 has 2, Row 2 has 4, Row 3 has 6). Predict how many you will need for Row 6.

extensions.title: Two-Dimensional Tessellation
extensions.description: Use two different pasta shapes to make a checkerboard grid pattern that repeats both left-to-right and top-to-bottom.

safetyNotes: Adult helper recommended for young learners.
Small counters like dried beans, coins, or dry pasta are choking hazards for children under 3 years old.
Dry pasta and beans are for learning manipulation only; remind learners not to eat raw materials.

concepts.name: Pattern Core
concepts.briefDefinition: The shortest group of shapes, colors, or sounds that repeats over and over without changing.
concepts.diagramHighlight: The bracket under the first red circle, blue square, and yellow star

inContext.scenario: When making a friendship bracelet with beads that go red, green, red, green...

concepts.name: Repeating Cycle

inContext.scenario: Clapping to a dance beat that goes 'clap, stomp, stomp, clap, stomp, stomp'...

data.title: Repeating Patterns vs. Growing Patterns
data.intro: Let us explore two fun kinds of patterns! A repeating pattern goes round and round like a song on loop, while a growing pattern gets bigger step by step like building a tall tower.

item1.name: Repeating Pattern
item1.description: A pattern that has a core which copies itself over and over again without changing its size.
item1.visualPrompt: Red square, blue circle, red square, blue circle in a line
points: The same shapes or colors repeat in order.
It stays the exact same size every time it loops.

item2.name: Growing Pattern
item2.description: A pattern where something is added at every step so it gets bigger and bigger.
item2.visualPrompt: One block, then two blocks, then three blocks in a staircase shape
points: It grows larger with every new step.
You can figure out what comes next by adding more.

synthesis.mainInsight: While repeating patterns loop the same items over and over, growing patterns change size by adding more pieces with each new step.
keyDifferences: Repeating patterns stay the same size, but growing patterns get bigger every time.
Repeating patterns copy the exact same core unit, while growing patterns add a new amount at each step.
keySimilarities: Both kinds of patterns follow a clear rule so you can always guess what comes next.
Both types of patterns use shapes, numbers, or objects in a set order.
synthesis.commonMisconception: Thinking that any pattern that has more objects is just repeating, instead of noticing that it is actually growing step by step.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use a repeating pattern when you want to make decorations like a colorful border that stays the same.
whenToUse.item2Context: Use a growing pattern when you want to build something that gets taller or larger, like stair steps or block towers.

gates.question: A repeating pattern gets bigger and bigger at every step like a staircase.
gates.rationale: That is incorrect! A repeating pattern stays the same size as it loops, while a growing pattern is the one that gets bigger step by step.

gates.question: Both repeating patterns and growing patterns follow a rule that helps you figure out what comes next.
gates.rationale: Spot on! Both types of patterns follow a special rule or order, which is how we know what shape or number belongs next.

cards.title: Repeating Pattern
cards.subheading: A line of shapes or colors that repeats again and again!
cards.definition: A repeating pattern is an orderly line of items, like colored blocks or shapes, arranged so that the exact same sequence happens over and over without changing.

conceptElements.detail: Red, Blue, Red, Blue shows a 2-part repeating sequence.
conceptElements.label: Simple Example

conceptElements.detail: Because it repeats, you can always guess what block belongs where!
conceptElements.label: Predictable Order

cards.timelineContext: Step 1 in Pattern Power: Spotting when a row of blocks follows a repeating rule rather than random mixing.
cards.originStory: Ancient basket weavers discovered that alternating light reeds and dark reeds in the same order made their woven baskets strong, durable, and eye-catching.
cards.curiosityNote: You can make a repeating pattern with sounds! Try clapping and tapping your knees: Clap, Tap, Clap, Tap!
cards.visualPrompt: A straight row of bright wooden blocks on a clean desk: Red cube, Blue sphere, Red cube, Blue sphere, Red cube, Blue sphere lined up evenly.

cards.title: Pattern Core (The Unit)
cards.subheading: The special chunk that repeats to build the whole pattern!
cards.definition: The core is the shortest group of blocks or shapes that repeats. Once you find the core, you have found the secret recipe of the pattern.

conceptElements.detail: The core is the smallest chunk that repeats from start to finish.
conceptElements.label: The Building Block

conceptElements.detail: In Yellow-Green-Green, Yellow-Green-Green, the core is Yellow-Green-Green.
conceptElements.label: Core Example

conceptElements.detail: Put your fingers around the first full repeat to isolate the core.
conceptElements.label: Find the Unit

cards.timelineContext: Step 2 in Pattern Power: Finding the repeating core so you know the exact rule of the pattern.
cards.originStory: Printmakers carve one single stamp design and press it repeatedly across fabric to make wallpaper and clothing prints.
cards.curiosityNote: A core can be 2 blocks long (AB), 3 blocks long (ABC or AAB), or even longer!
cards.visualPrompt: Snap cubes connected in a row: Yellow, Green, Green, Yellow, Green, Green. A bright glowing dotted rectangle frames the first Yellow, Green, Green set to show it as the core.

cards.title: Continue the Pattern
cards.subheading: Add the correct next blocks to keep the line going!
cards.definition: To continue a pattern means to look back at the repeating core and add the correct block or shape that comes next in the sequence.

conceptElements.detail: Say the pattern out loud to hear what block should land in the blank spot.
conceptElements.label: Ask What Comes Next

conceptElements.detail: Check if your new piece matches the start of the core.
conceptElements.label: Match the Core

conceptElements.detail: Place your block down and read the whole row again to make sure it sounds right.
conceptElements.label: Check Your Work

cards.timelineContext: Step 3 in Pattern Power: Using the core to extend, copy, and complete the row with your hands.
cards.originStory: Masons building brick walls learned that following the pattern layer by layer ensured the wall never tipped over.
cards.curiosityNote: As long as you have enough colored blocks, you can continue a repeating pattern all the way across your classroom floor!
cards.visualPrompt: A child's hand placing an orange plastic triangle into an empty spot at the end of a colorful shape line: Orange Triangle, Blue Hexagon, Orange Triangle, Blue Hexagon, with a glowing empty outline waiting for the next piece.

data.title: Kitchen Counter Pattern Lab: Repeating and Growing Patterns
data.subject: Math
data.overview: Become a pattern detective right in your own kitchen! By sorting and arranging everyday treasures like dried pasta, buttons, or coins, you will discover the secrets of repeating sequences and growing mathematical towers.
learningObjectives: Identify, describe, and extend simple repeating patterns (such as AB, ABB, and ABC) using physical objects and rhythmic speech.
Distinguish between repeating patterns and growing patterns by observing changes in quantity.
Create and predict the next term in a growing pattern using counting and visual models.

substitutes: a straight edge of a kitchen table

steps.title: Sort Your Treasure Collection
steps.instruction: Place your different counters into separate small bowls so each kind of object has its own home.
steps.tip: Keep each group separated clearly so you can grab items quickly when building your sequence.

steps.title: Build an AB Repeating Train
steps.instruction: Line up your objects in an AB pattern along your paper strip by alternating one of Type A, then one of Type B, and repeat: A, B, A, B, A, B.

checkpoint.question: Touch each item and read it aloud with a rhythm: 'Bow-tie, Macaroni, Bow-tie, Macaroni!' Does your rhythm stay the same?

steps.scienceNote: The 'core unit' is the shortest chunk that repeats. Here, the unit is just two items: [A, B].

steps.title: Level Up to an ABB Pattern
steps.instruction: Clear your line. Now build a new sequence using one Type A object followed by two Type B objects: A, B, B, A, B, B, A, B, B.

checkpoint.question: How many items are in one complete core unit of an ABB pattern?

steps.tip: Try whispering the single item and clapping twice for the double item to feel the rhythm.

steps.title: The Disappearing Piece Mystery
steps.instruction: Close your eyes while your helper removes one object from your pattern. Open your eyes, chant the pattern out loud, and guess the missing piece.

checkpoint.question: What clues did the neighboring pieces give you to help identify the missing object?

steps.title: Switch to a Growing Pattern
steps.instruction: Clear your line to start something new! Place 1 penny in the first row. Directly underneath, make a second row with 2 pennies. Make a third row with 3 pennies.
steps.scienceNote: Repeating patterns repeat the same cycle again and again, but growing patterns change by a regular mathematical rule each step.

steps.title: Predict and Extend the Growth
steps.instruction: Look closely at your penny staircase. Use your counters to build the 4th row and the 5th row following the same growth rule.

checkpoint.question: How many counters did you need to make the 5th row?

steps.tip: Notice how each step adds exactly one more counter than the step before it.

reflectionPrompts.question: What is the difference between how your pasta train looked in Step 2 compared to how your penny staircase looked in Step 5?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Distinguish between repeating patterns and growing patterns by observing changes in quantity.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether the sizes stay the same or get bigger and bigger as you move forward.

reflectionPrompts.question: If you wanted to build the 10th row of your growing staircase, how could you figure out how many counters you need without building all the rows first?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Create and predict the next term in a growing pattern using counting and visual models.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look at the row number and compare it to the number of counters in that row.

reflectionPrompts.question: Where can you spot repeating patterns or growing patterns in your daily life or nature?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Identify, describe, and extend simple repeating patterns using physical objects.
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look at bathroom tiles, clothing stripes, tree branches, or musical beats.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Take a photo looking down at your finished growing staircase alongside your favorite repeating pattern chain.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: My pattern lab results! My repeating pattern rule was ______ and row 5 of my growing pattern had ______ pieces!

data.title: Repeating Patterns vs. Growing Patterns
data.intro: Let us explore two fun kinds of patterns! A repeating pattern goes round and round like a song on loop, while a growing pattern gets bigger step by step like building a tall tower.

item1.name: Repeating Pattern
item1.description: A pattern that has a core which copies itself over and over again without changing its size.
item1.visualPrompt: Red square, blue circle, red square, blue circle in a line
points: The same shapes or colors repeat in order.
It stays the exact same size every time it loops.

item2.name: Growing Pattern
item2.description: A pattern where something is added at every step so it gets bigger and bigger.
item2.visualPrompt: One block, then two blocks, then three blocks in a staircase shape
points: It grows larger with every new step.
You can figure out what comes next by adding more.

synthesis.mainInsight: While repeating patterns loop the same items over and over, growing patterns change size by adding more pieces with each new step.
keyDifferences: Repeating patterns stay the same size, but growing patterns get bigger every time.
Repeating patterns copy the exact same core unit, while growing patterns add a new amount at each step.
keySimilarities: Both kinds of patterns follow a clear rule so you can always guess what comes next.
Both types of patterns use shapes, numbers, or objects in a set order.
synthesis.commonMisconception: Thinking that any pattern that has more objects is just repeating, instead of noticing that it is actually growing step by step.

whenToUse.item1Context: Use a repeating pattern when you want to make decorations like a colorful border that stays the same.
whenToUse.item2Context: Use a growing pattern when you want to build something that gets taller or larger, like stair steps or block towers.

gates.question: A repeating pattern gets bigger and bigger at every step like a staircase.
gates.rationale: That is incorrect! A repeating pattern stays the same size as it loops, while a growing pattern is the one that gets bigger step by step.

gates.question: Both repeating patterns and growing patterns follow a rule that helps you figure out what comes next.
gates.rationale: Spot on! Both types of patterns follow a special rule or order, which is how we know what shape or number belongs next.

data.title: Growing Patterns with Kangaroo Leaps
data.description: Create your own growing pattern that gets bigger step by step by hopping on the number line.

character.imagePrompt: A friendly cartoon kangaroo wearing a red scarf, ready to hop.

challenges.instruction: Watch the kangaroo hop by 5s and count along!
challenges.hint: Listen to the rhythm: 5, 10, 15...

challenges.instruction: Fill in the missing numbers as the kangaroo builds the growing pattern.
challenges.hint: Each hop adds 5 more to the total.

challenges.instruction: The kangaroo is at 10. Where is the next landing in the growing pattern?
challenges.hint: Add 5 to 10 to find the next spot.

challenges.instruction: Look at the pattern on the number line. How much does the pattern grow with each jump?
challenges.hint: Count the tick marks between each landing.
challenges.narration: Discover the hidden skip value of this growing pattern.

challenges.instruction: The kangaroo is at 20. Where is the next landing?
challenges.hint: Add 5 more to 20.
challenges.narration: What number comes after 20 in our growing pattern?

data.title: Growing Staircase Patterns

challenges.instruction: Build a small growing step pattern starting with 1 block and adding 1 block each time.

challenges.instruction: Create a pattern that grows by adding 2 blocks at each step.

challenges.narration: Now let's try a pattern that grows faster by adding two blocks each time.

challenges.instruction: Build a growing number sequence starting at 3 and adding 3 each time.
